plan: [ This is strategically equivalent to a second‑price auction: the highest sealed bid wins and pays the second-highest bid. In such auctions, bidding one’s true value is a dominant strategy—it maximizes expected profit regardless of others’ strategies. Overbidding risks winning at a price above value; underbidding risks losing when winning would have yielded positive surplus. There is only 1 round and no history to learn from, so no adjustments are needed. Therefore, bid exactly my private value to ensure I win whenever price is below or equal to my value and avoid negative surplus. ]

[This auction is strategically equivalent to a second-price auction: the winner pays the second-highest sealed bid. The weakly dominant strategy is to bid one’s true private value. With a value of $3, bidding higher risks paying above value if others bid slightly above 3; bidding lower risks losing when the price would have been below 3. There is only one round and no history to exploit, so no dynamic adjustments. Therefore, bid exactly $3 to maximize expected profit.]

[ This is effectively a sealed-bid second-price auction (winner pays the second-highest sealed bid via the clock exit). With independent private values and risk-neutral preferences, the dominant strategy is to bid your true value to maximize expected profit over the long run. Overbidding risks paying more than value if the second-highest exceeds value; underbidding risks losing positive-surplus wins. With value 26 and no prior history to exploit, bid exactly 26. ]
